Abhor

/ab-HOR/ — stress on the second syllable, which rhymes with door · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To abhor something is to regard it with disgust and hatred — to loathe it so deeply that it almost makes you shudder.

Doctors who have seen its damage firsthand abhor the marketing of tobacco to teenagers.

Worked Example

A wildlife photographer spends months filming a herd of elephants, then discovers poachers have attacked the herd overnight; revulsion and hatred rise in her together, and she vows to publish every photograph of the crime.

Her feeling is not mild annoyance — it is hatred mixed with disgust, strong enough to make her act. That shuddering, moral loathing is exactly what abhor names. Because the disgust runs so deep, abhor is far more precise here than the plain word "dislike."

How Abhor Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

loathe

loathe: to hate with deep disgust — the closest everyday match for abhor

despise

despise: to look down on something as worthless or beneath you

hate

hate: the plain, all-purpose word for strong dislike

Antonyms

adore

adore: to love something deeply and enthusiastically

cherish

cherish: to hold something dear and guard it carefully

How Strong Is It? — dislike → despise → loathe → abhor

dislike vs. abhor

dislike vs. abhor: Dislike is far weaker than abhor: it is a simple preference against something, with no disgust in it at all.

despise vs. abhor

despise vs. abhor: Despise is strong contempt — looking down on something — but abhor goes further, adding a shudder of disgust.

loathe vs. abhor

loathe vs. abhor: Loathe comes very close, but abhor is the peak: hatred so deep it borders on horror, making you recoil.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ab-

Prefix — ab-: away, from (Latin)

Root — horrere

Root — horrere: to shudder, to bristle with fear or disgust (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Ab (away) + horrere (to shudder) — to abhor something is literally to shudder away from it. The word paints a picture: disgust so strong that your whole body pulls back. That same shudder hides inside 'horror,' 'horrible,' and 'horrify,' which all grow from the very same root.

Use the root in a new word: horrify

Use the root in a new word: horrify: The health inspector was horrified to find mold spreading through the restaurant's walls, and he shuddered as he wrote up his report.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / strong

Abhor is one of the strongest dislike words in English — reserve it for things that stir real moral disgust, like cruelty or injustice. Saying you abhor broccoli sounds comically dramatic; for everyday preferences, the plain word "dislike" is the simpler, better choice.
